newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Russian ship beats Sierra Leone embargo.
newsitem.headline: Russian ship beats Sierra Leone embargo.

text.p: A Russian ship carrying 6,800 tonnes of rice docked in Freetown on Thursday, hours after West African foreign ministers decided to tighten an embargo against Sierra Leone's army junta.
A huge cheer went up on the waterfront where crowds of Sierra Leoneans desperate for food had gathered as the Russia-flag Ivanov beat a Nigerian blockade to dock with the rice.
A navy boat sent by the military junta which seized power in a coup on May 25 escorted the ship into port, witnesses said.
"This is the first cargo boat to dock in Sierra Leone since the coup," a harbour official said.
But despite the short-term relief from the shipment, the blockade and the continuing standoff between the junta and Nigerian troops looked likely to aggravate Sierra Leone's woes.
Once a leading world exporter of bauxite and rutile and a major producer of diamonds, Sierra Leone now ranks among the poorest countries on earth.
Five years of civil war forced mines to close and foreign operators to flee. Agriculture is devastated with more than a third of the population of just over four million displaced.

The coup two months ago triggered massive looting and mayhem, forcing Lebanese and Asians who dominated business to flee. Most shops and banks remain closed despite repeated orders from the military for their owners to reopen them.

The 16-nation Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) clamped an economic blockade on the country in an attempt to force the junta to hand back power to ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who is exiled in nearby Guinea.
Diplomatic talks broke down on Wednesday and an ECOWAS ministerial committee of Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea and Ivory Coast endorsed a tightenening of a land, air and sea blockade.

Nigeria is the backbone of the military arm of ECOWAS, known as ECOMOG. Nigerian Air Force units control the international airport outside Freetown and warships patrol offshore. Army units are on the land border with Liberia and inside Sierra Leone at Kenema, on the main road into Freetown from Guinea.
Junta spokesman Allieu Kamara said the military had ordered harbour authorities to get the rice to market rapidly.

"The shipment of rice will last the country for about two to three months. We are also expecting a shipment of fuel, especially petrol and kerosene, to arrive in Freetown by ship over the weekend," Kamara added.

The ship's arrival marked the second defiant act by the junta in as many days. Military leader Major Johnny Paul Koroma set back negotiations on Wednesday night by announcing that he would stay in power until November 2001.
Talks between the ministers and Koroma's envoys on restoring the elected government peacefully immediately broke off in the Ivorian commercial capital Abidjan.

Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi who chaired the talks lashed out at Koroma's radio and television broadcast, saying "it is an affront to ECOWAS, it is an affront to Africa, it is an affront to the international community."
He read out a declaration by his committee ordering a stepped-up blockade as junta envoys listened impassively.

Delegates said that with fuel for power generation and basic transport running short in Freetown and elsewhere, and with prices of basic foods soaring, the aim was to put pressure on the government while stopping short of the military option.
Nigerian troops tried to reverse the coup militarily on June 2 but soldiers loyal to Koroma and former rebels who rallied to the coup foiled the poorly-coordinated attempt.
No ECOWAS member has shown any willingness to join in any further military action to reinstate Kabbah.
